# Rational anchored templates for boundary martingales

This is a finite-template refinement of the coupling in
`candidate 7278f286325c46c7`. It is a theorem
about a given coupling, not an existence argument for a depth minimum or
an OC depth bound. A search of the existing anchored-representation and
boundary-coupling notes found the ingredients separately, but no prior
statement of this measure-preserving refinement.

The intermediate measure retains a finite template label. Without that
label, several templates can have the same intermediate physical point;
the corresponding unmarked row then has a mixture of templates. On flat
faces the intermediate physical point need not equal the input point.

## 1. Setup and statement

Let P be a nonempty finite subset of Z^n. Write s=dim aff(P). For each
p in P let K_p be a nonempty compact convex subset of R^d, where d>=1.
Assume actual-fiber compatibility:

    sum_q a_q K_q subset K_p whenever
    a_q>=0, sum_q a_q=1, sum_q a_q q=p.                 (1)

In particular, (1) holds if these are the sections at P of a convex set.
No full-dimensionality, boundary smoothness, or lattice completeness of
P is needed for the present theorem. Let h_p(u)=max_(x in K_p) u.x,
F_p(u)={x in K_p:u.x=h_p(u)}, and

    N={(u,p,x):u in S^(d-1), p in P, x in F_p(u)}.

The set N is compact. Its physical coordinate is w(u,p,x)=(p,x).
Suppose gamma is a finite nonnegative Borel measure on N times N with
first marginal nu and second marginal eta, satisfying

    input normal = output normal, gamma-almost everywhere,
    integral f(a)[w(b)-w(a)] dgamma(a,b)=0              (2)

for every bounded Borel f on N. Thus gamma is a normal-preserving physical
martingale. The zero-mass case has the zero factorization below.

For p in P define its anchored representation polytope

    A_p={a in R^P:a_q>=0, sum a_q=1, sum a_q q=p}.

List its vertices as alpha^(p,r), 1<=r<=R_p. These are rational vectors;
each has at most s+1 positive coordinates. There exists an integer D>=1,
depending only on P, such that every D alpha^(p,r)_q is an integer.

**Theorem.** There exist a finite nonnegative measure nu-hat on the marked
intermediate space

    N-hat={(u,p,z,r):(u,p,z) in N, 1<=r<=R_p},

a coupling gamma_1 from nu to nu-hat, and a coupling gamma_2 from nu-hat
to eta, with the following properties.

1. Both couplings preserve the normal exactly and are martingales in the
   physical coordinates. The first coupling also preserves the base p.
2. For every p,r,q, the first marginal of the restriction of gamma_2 to
   input base/template (p,r) and output base q equals

       alpha^(p,r)_q times nu-hat restricted to (p,r).  (3)

   Thus, conditioned on the marked input, its output base distribution
   is exactly one of the finitely many rational templates.
3. There is a refinement of the ORIGINAL gamma carrying the extra label
   r whose projection back to its original input/output pair is gamma.
   In particular the full target law eta is preserved, including its
   conditional continuous-coordinate distributions at each base.
4. Every template used with positive mass at a source (u,p,x) is active:

       sum_q alpha^(p,r)_q h_q(u)=h_p(u).              (4)

   Its intermediate point lies in F_p(u). In fact

       sum_q alpha^(p,r)_q F_q(u) subset F_p(u).        (5)

5. If nu-almost every input x is an extreme point of K_p, then the first
   coupling makes no physical movement: its intermediate point equals
   x. This applies, in particular, when every K_p is a strictly convex
   full-dimensional body.

Forgetting the label in nu-hat yields a two-stage unmarked martingale
nu -> nu' -> eta, still normal-preserving. Assertion (3), as an assertion
of a single template per row, is made on the marked space.

## 2. The finite rational template list and a Borel decomposition

Form the integer matrix B whose column indexed by q is (1,q). Then
A_p={a>=0:Ba=(1,p)}. It is nonempty, closed and bounded, since it is a
closed subset of the probability simplex.

An element a of A_p is a vertex if and only if the columns of B indexed
by its positive support are linearly independent. If they are dependent,
choose a nonzero vector v on that support with Bv=0. Both a+epsilon v
and a-epsilon v are nonnegative for small epsilon>0, giving a nontrivial
segment through a. Conversely, if those columns are independent and
a=(b+c)/2 with b,c in A_p, nonnegativity forces both b and c to vanish
outside the support of a, and B(b-c)=0 forces b=c.

There are finitely many supports. For an independent support, its unique
solution is rational: select a nonsingular square minor of its integer
column matrix and use the adjugate formula. Its support size is at most
rank(B)=s+1. Therefore there are finitely many rational vertices, and
the least common multiple of their denominators gives D.

For completeness every a in A_p is a convex combination of these
vertices. If its support is dependent, the preceding null direction v
has both positive and negative entries because sum v_q=0. Move in each
direction until a coordinate first becomes zero. The resulting two
points have strictly smaller supports and a lies on their segment.
Repeating this finite induction on support size proves the assertion.

We next fix one Borel choice of convex coefficients

    theta^(p)_r(a)>=0,
    sum_r theta^(p)_r(a)=1,
    sum_r theta^(p)_r(a) alpha^(p,r)=a.                (6)

There is no parameter-dependent measurable-selection theorem hidden
here. Enumerate all affinely independent nonempty sublists of the finite
vertex list. Their convex hulls cover A_p: any convex representation
with affine dependence can have one coefficient eliminated by moving
along that dependence, and iteration gives an independent sublist.
Use the first listed sublist whose convex hull contains a. Each such
convex hull is closed, so the regions on which the first sublist is
selected are Borel. On that sublist the barycentric coordinates are
unique affine functions on its affine span; extend each to an affine
function on the whole coordinate space. Set all unselected coefficients
to zero. This gives (6), with Borel, piecewise affine theta functions.

The template list contains the self-template e_p. Every other vertex
has alpha_p=0: if 0<alpha_p<1, remove its self mass to write it as the
nontrivial convex combination alpha_p e_p+(1-alpha_p) beta, beta in A_p.

## 3. Row moments without conditional probability kernels

Write a=(u,p,x) for the input of gamma. For each target base q let
gamma_q be the restriction of gamma to outputs of base q. Its first
marginal is dominated by nu, and hence is w_q nu for a nonnegative
Borel Radon--Nikodym derivative w_q. The vector measure

    E -> integral_(a in E, output base q) y dgamma(a,b)

is also absolutely continuous with respect to nu; write its Borel
vector density as m_q(a). Since the output y lies in the fixed compact
K_q, |m_q|<=C_q w_q almost everywhere for a bound C_q on |y| in K_q.
The marginal and moment conditions (2) give, almost everywhere,

    sum_q w_q=1,  sum_q w_q q=p,  sum_q m_q=x.         (7)

For w_q>0 put y_q=m_q/w_q. Then

    y_q in F_q(u).                                    (8)

Here are all measurability/support details for (8). For each rational
vector v, the target inequality v.y<=h_q(v) implies
v.m_q<=h_q(v)w_q almost everywhere, by testing the corresponding measure
inequality on every Borel input set. Intersect the countably many
full-measure sets over q and rational v. Density of rational vectors and
continuity of support functions then show y_q in K_q. Normal preservation
and the output's membership in N give

    u(a).m_q(a)=h_q(u(a))w_q(a)

almost everywhere. Indeed multiply each coordinate RN identity by the
bounded Borel function u_i(a), sum, and use the pointwise equality
u(a).y=h_q(u(a)) under gamma_q. This proves (8). When w_q=0, set y_q
equal to any fixed point of K_q. This choice is Borel and will never
affect a positive term below.

Take one common Borel full-nu-measure input set on which (7)--(8) hold.
Discard its null complement from the formulas. As P is finite, these
are only finitely or countably many null-set exclusions. All eventual
measures retain the original marginals exactly.

For such an input let theta_r(a)=theta^(p)_r(w(a)), using Section 2, and
put

    z_r(a)=sum_q alpha^(p,r)_q y_q(a) if theta_r(a)>0;
    z_r(a)=x otherwise.                               (9)

These functions are Borel. If theta_r>0 and alpha^(p,r)_q>0, equation
(6) forces w_q>0. Thus every positive summand in (9) satisfies (8).
Compatibility (1) gives z_r in K_p and gives, for every template,

    sum_q alpha^(p,r)_q h_q(u)<=h_p(u).               (10)

The theta-weighted average of the left sides of (10) is
sum_q w_q h_q(u)=u.sum_q m_q=u.x=h_p(u). Therefore every positive-theta
term has equality. This proves (4), z_r in F_p(u), and (5): any choice
of points in the component support faces has the same supporting value
and lies in K_p by (1). Finally

    sum_r theta_r z_r=sum_q w_q y_q=sum_q m_q=x.       (11)

Terms with w_q=0 vanish throughout.

## 4. The exact refinement and the two couplings

For each p,r,q define a measure on original input/output pairs by

    dDelta_(p,r,q)(a,b)
      = 1_(input base p) [theta_r(a) alpha^(p,r)_q / w_q(a)]
          dgamma_q(a,b),                             (12)

where the bracket is defined to be zero when w_q=0. It is a nonnegative
Borel function, and it is at most one: theta_r alpha_q<=w_q. Thus (12)
defines a finite measure without any integrability issue.

For every q, the sum over p,r of the densities in (12) equals one
gamma_q-almost everywhere, because sum_r theta_r alpha_q=w_q and the
first marginal w_q nu gives no mass to {w_q=0}. Consequently

    sum_(p,r,q) Delta_(p,r,q)=gamma.                  (13)

Keeping p,r as a mark in this sum proves assertion 3. Its first marginal
for fixed p,r,q is

    1_(input base p) theta_r alpha^(p,r)_q nu.         (14)

Moreover, its conditional continuous first-moment measure on input
sets has density theta_r alpha^(p,r)_q y_q. This follows directly from
the RN definition of m_q; multiplication by the bounded density in
(12) is legitimate. No disintegration has been used.

Define nu-hat as the sum, over p,r, of the pushforward of
1_(input base p) theta_r nu under a -> (u,p,z_r(a),r).
Define gamma_1 by the same construction while retaining a as its first
coordinate. Equations (9)--(11) show that gamma_1 preserves the normal
and base and has physical conditional mean (p,x). This conditional-mean
statement can equivalently be checked against every bounded Borel
function of a using (11).

Push Delta_(p,r,q) forward by

    (a,b) -> ((u,p,z_r(a),r), b)

and sum to obtain gamma_2. Formula (14), summed over q, proves its first
marginal is nu-hat. Formula (13) proves its second marginal is eta.
Formula (14) itself proves (3). Its normal is preserved because it was
preserved in gamma. For any bounded Borel test f on N-hat, its physical
mean increment equals the integral against nu of the sum of

    1_(input base p) theta_r f(u,p,z_r,r)
        [sum_q alpha^(p,r)_q(q,y_q) - (p,z_r)],

which is zero by the anchored equations and (9). Thus gamma_2 is a
physical martingale. This verifies all assertions involving marginals,
normal support, and conditional means even when different original
inputs produce the same marked intermediate point.

Notice the distinction between (13) and a Markov composition claim.
The original gamma is the projection of the marked refinement retaining
the original input. If one forgets that input and subsequently composes
only the two projected couplings gamma_1 and gamma_2, additional mixing
at coincident intermediate points can occur. No equality of that Markov
composition with gamma is asserted or needed; the full target law is
preserved exactly in both constructions.

## 5. Extreme sources and the indispensable flat-face qualification

If x is extreme in K_p, equation (11), with z_r in K_p, forces z_r=x
for every positive theta_r. For a strictly convex full-dimensional
K_p, every support face F_p(u) is a singleton, giving the stated special
case. The proof also works when only nu-almost every input is extreme;
no condition on uncharged boundary points is needed.

The fixed-source conclusion is false on general flat faces. Take

    P={0,1,2}, K_0=K_1=K_2=[-1,1]^2,
    u=(0,1), input (p,x)=(1,(0,1)).

Let its target law have atoms

    (0,(-1,1)) with mass 1/4,
    (1,( 1,1)) with mass 1/2,
    (2,(-1,1)) with mass 1/4.

This is a normal-preserving physical martingale, and the fibers are
actual sections of [0,2] times [-1,1]^2. The anchored polytope at 1 is

    {(t,1-2t,t):0<=t<=1/2},

whose two vertices are e_1 and (1/2,0,1/2). The target base weights are
their unique mixture with coefficients 1/2,1/2. The intermediate means
are respectively (1,1) and (-1,1), each with mass 1/2. A self-template
row retaining the original (0,1) cannot use the prescribed target law:
the only target at base 1 is (1,1), which has the wrong continuous mean.
Nonnegativity prevents canceling this atom with any unlisted target.
Hence even existence of some extreme-template splitting at the unchanged
source, with this same target law, is impossible.

## 6. Exact integer interpretation and limits of the conclusion

Put n^(p,r)_q=D alpha^(p,r)_q. Every marked row uses one of the finitely
many nonnegative integer patterns

    sum_q n^(p,r)_q=D,  sum_q n^(p,r)_q q=Dp.

For an active pattern, compatibility and (4) give

    sum_q n^(p,r)_q F_q(u) subset D F_p(u),

where sums are Minkowski sums and D F_p is scalar dilation. This is an
exact balanced integer multiset interpretation of the row. It neither
forces D to be a power of two nor forces a midpoint representation.
Although integer coordinates make the templates rational, lattice
completeness was not used; arbitrary rational base sets admit the same
conclusion after a common scaling. Therefore the factorization alone
cannot supply the missing parity-budget inequality or an OC center.
